plan.contextChunk: This figure places three small drawings in a row, each pairing a circle with a straight line rendered as a blue double-headed arrow, to enumerate how many points the two curves can share. In the leftmost drawing the circle is orange and the blue line passes above and to the left of it without ever touching the rim; the label beneath reads "No solutions." In the center drawing the circle is green and the blue line rises steeply from lower left to upper right, grazing the circle at a single point on its upper-left edge, which is marked with a filled black dot; the label beneath reads "One solution." In the rightmost drawing the circle is red and the blue line cuts through it, entering at the lower left and exiting at the upper right; the upper-right crossing is visibly marked with a filled black dot while the second crossing is implied by the line passing through the circle. The label beneath reads "Two solutions." The three panels hold the circle size and the line's slope fixed and change how far the line sits from the center, so the number of circle-line intersections is the variable. Together they lay out the complete range of outcomes for a system built from a circle and a line.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A circle and a line can intersect in only three ways — not at all, at exactly one point (tangent), or at two points — so a circle-line system has zero, one, or two solutions.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the source figure as a purely static drop-in replacement: three equal panels in a horizontal row, each containing one circle and one line. Everything is drawn in uniform thin black strokes — no colors, no varying line widths, no filled dots at intersection points (the visual crossing of line and circle alone implies the solutions). All circles are the same size; all lines share the same steep positive slope and extend past the circle as in the source. Left panel: line sits above-left of the circle, clearly not touching it. Center panel: line grazes the circle's upper-left rim at a single tangent point. Right panel: line passes through the circle from lower left to upper right, crossing the rim twice. Beneath each panel, a centered label reads 'No solutions', 'One solution', and 'Two solutions' respectively, positioned exactly as in the source image. No explore panel, no sliders, no toggles, no buttons, no highlight rings, no equations, no annotations — the composition must match the static textbook figure exactly.

plan.concept: A system made of one circle and one line can have zero, one, or two solutions, and which case occurs is determined entirely by the distance from the circle's center to the line compared with the radius.
elements: three side-by-side panels, each containing one circle and one blue double-headed arrow line
left panel: orange circle, blue line passing above-left of the circle without touching it, label 'No solutions'
center panel: green circle, steep blue line grazing the circle at one point on the upper-left rim, filled black dot at the tangent point, label 'One solution'
right panel: red circle, blue line cutting through the circle from lower left to upper right, filled black dot at the upper-right crossing (second crossing implied), label 'Two solutions'
equation view panel: circle equation, line equation, and discriminant value with its sign annotation (negative / zero / positive)
intersection-point markers (filled black dots) that appear/disappear as the line moves

interactions.label: Distance from center to line
interactions.teaches: As the line slides parallel to itself toward the center, the intersection count passes continuously from none, through exactly one (tangent, when distance equals radius), to two — so distance versus radius is what decides the number of solutions

interactions.label: Step through cases
interactions.teaches: The three geometric cases — line misses the circle, line is tangent, line is secant — are the complete and exhaustive set of outcomes for a circle-line system

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The geometric count of intersection points corresponds exactly to the algebraic number of real solutions, signaled by the discriminant being negative, zero, or positive

demo_steps.title: No solutions
demo_steps.narration: The line sits too far from the center — its distance exceeds the radius — so it never touches the circle and the system has no solutions.

demo_steps.title: One solution (tangent)
demo_steps.narration: Slide the line inward until its distance from the center exactly equals the radius: it grazes the circle at a single point — the tangent case, one solution.

demo_steps.title: Two solutions (secant)
demo_steps.narration: Push the line closer than the radius and it cuts through the circle, crossing the rim twice — the secant case, two solutions.

demo_steps.title: Connect to algebra
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the equation view: substituting the line into the circle's equation gives a quadratic whose discriminant is negative, zero, or positive in exactly the three cases you just saw.

plan.keyInsight: Comparing the center-to-line distance with the radius — equivalently, the sign of the discriminant after substitution — completely determines whether a circle-line system has zero, one, or two solutions.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Three equal panels in a horizontal row with generous whitespace, matching the textbook figure. All circles the same size; all lines the same steep positive slope (lower-left to upper-right), drawn as blue double-headed arrows extending beyond the circle. Color-code the cases: orange circle for no solutions, green for one solution, red for two solutions. Centered serif labels beneath each panel: 'No solutions', 'One solution', 'Two solutions'. Intersection points are small filled black dots; show both crossing dots in the secant case even though the original marks only one, so the count is unambiguous. The slider moves the line perpendicular to itself (offset from center) across all panels simultaneously or within a single enlarged active panel; mark the tangent case distinctly when distance equals radius. In Equation view, show a generic circle equation, the line equation, the substituted quadratic, and a color-coded discriminant readout (negative/zero/positive) synced to the current offset.

demo_steps.title: Three cases at a glance
demo_steps.narration: All three possibilities are shown at once: the line misses the circle entirely, grazes it at one point, or cuts through it at two. The dots marking intersections are visible from the start.

demo_steps.title: Focus: no solutions
demo_steps.narration: Highlighting the left panel: the line's distance from the center exceeds the radius, so it never touches the circle — no solutions.

demo_steps.title: Focus: one solution
demo_steps.narration: Highlighting the center panel: the line's distance exactly equals the radius, so it is tangent — one solution, marked by the single dot.

demo_steps.title: Focus: two solutions
demo_steps.narration: Highlighting the right panel: the line's distance is less than the radius, so it crosses the rim twice — two solutions, marked by both dots.

demo_steps.title: Sweep continuously in the explore panel
demo_steps.narration: Drag the distance slider in the explore panel: the intersection dots vanish, merge into one, and split into two as d passes through r — the three fixed panels are snapshots of this single sweep.

demo_steps.title: Connect to algebra
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the equation view: substituting the line into the circle's equation gives a quadratic whose discriminant is negative, zero, or positive in exactly the three regimes you just swept through.
